# Airport Medical Clinic Offers Convenient Care for Travelers

**ATLANTA, Georgia (CNN)** — After his flight touched down in Atlanta from Sarasota, Florida, Stephen Plumlee began experiencing nausea and lightheadedness. Rather than being rushed to a downtown hospital, paramedics wheeled him to a medical facility located right inside the terminal of the world's busiest airport.

This walk-in medical center, called The AeroClinic, represents part of an expanding trend of accessible healthcare options popping up in retail spaces and drugstores nationwide. The facility provides affordable, rapid treatment for both passengers and airport staff—a workforce numbering roughly 55,000. According to Dr. Dominic Mack, the clinic's chief medical officer, "We're kind of the stop in between the hospital during your travels."

Positioned somewhere between compact neighborhood clinics and the larger, established urgent-care centers that have operated for decades, The AeroClinic charges approximately $80 for consultations with a doctor or physician assistant regarding minor conditions like sore throats, digestive issues, or headaches.

This affordability drew Derrick Gross, a medical sales rep based in Atlanta whose job keeps him traveling at least three days weekly. Lacking time for regular doctor visits, he noticed the clinic's signage during a layover and booked an appointment on the spot. Physician assistant Sabrina Jackson spent roughly 20 minutes running diagnostic tests to identify what was triggering his headaches. When results showed nothing alarming, she prescribed ibuprofen. "I took a chance by coming here today and I'm satisfied," Gross remarked, noting he planned to follow up with his regular physician.

Mack explained that Gross represents a common scenario among his patients. With 250,000 travelers passing through Atlanta's Hartsfield airport daily, illness is inevitable—yet many either postpone treatment or skip it entirely.

Former U.S. Surgeon General David Satcher, who logs extensive air travel himself, recognizes this gap firsthand. "I've traveled almost 40,000 miles in the last month and I know there are a lot of people who spend time in airports and a lot of people don't get the care they need," he noted. A member of the American Academy of Family Physicians, Satcher supports the airport clinic model—provided patients maintain ongoing relationships with their home physicians. He also sits on The AeroClinic's board and was among the private company's founding investors.

Satcher emphasized the clinic's limitations: "This is not the place to go when you're having chest pains. ... But obviously, if you have a minor illness, this is an opportunity to seek care while you're traveling and not have to wait until you get back home."

Beyond treating immediate ailments, the clinic's staff of 12 also handles preventive services—physical examinations, standard vaccinations, and management of ongoing health conditions. Some insurance plans are accepted at the facility.

Expansion plans are underway, with a second AeroClinic location set to open this fall at Philadelphia's airport. The team also intends to set up mobile flu-shot stations throughout the concourses. Currently, patients must exit the secure zone of the airport to access clinic services.

For Plumlee, this minor hassle was worthwhile. "I was so out of it, I didn't know what was happening. But everyone has been very helpful," he said. Following a couple hours of rest, doctors determined his symptoms stemmed from an inner-ear balance disorder. He received medication to manage the return flight before departing.

"This has been good," Plumlee reflected. "It's been fine to be able to do it in the airport, not have to go to some other part of the city and find my way back."

*E-mail to a friend.*

*Judy Fortin is a correspondent with CNN Medical News.*

# Airport Health Clinic Offers Travelers a New Kind of Layover

*By CNN Staff*

**ATLANTA** — Between gate changes, security lines, and delayed connections, Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport now offers travelers something unexpected: a full-service medical clinic.

The clinic, called TravelWell Health, opened its doors last month in Concourse D, marking one of the first comprehensive urgent care facilities embedded directly within a major U.S. airport terminal. The 2,400-square-foot space includes exam rooms, a small pharmacy, telehealth stations, and even a quiet room for travelers managing chronic conditions like diabetes or anxiety-related flare-ups.

"We treat this like any other neighborhood urgent care, except our patients are usually checking their watches," said Dr. Priya Nathan, the clinic's medical director. "Someone might have an ear infection that's made worse by cabin pressure, or they forgot their insulin in checked luggage. We're here to solve problems fast, because for a lot of these people, missing a flight isn't an option."

## A Different Kind of Patient Base

Unlike traditional clinics, TravelWell's patient population changes by the hour. Staff say they see everything from minor injuries and allergic reactions to travelers experiencing early signs of blood clots after long-haul flights.

Denise Alvarez, a 41-year-old marketing consultant from Chicago, found herself at the clinic after a 14-hour flight from Seoul left her calf swollen and painful.

"I almost just powered through it," Alvarez said. "But my leg was so swollen I couldn't get my shoe back on. The nurse practitioner recognized the signs of a possible DVT right away and got me to a hospital instead of letting me board my connecting flight. I probably would have ignored it otherwise."

Alvarez was diagnosed with deep vein thrombosis at a nearby hospital and is now recovering. "That clinic probably saved me from a much scarier situation at 30,000 feet," she said.

Other cases are less dramatic but no less disruptive to travelers' plans. Mark Delgado, a 58-year-old business traveler, stopped by after developing a sinus infection mid-trip.

"I was ready to just suffer through three more flights," Delgado said. "Instead, I was in and out in 40 minutes with antibiotics from their pharmacy. It's such a simple idea — I don't know why every airport doesn't have this."

## Filling a Gap in Travel Medicine

Experts say the clinic addresses a long-standing gap in airport infrastructure. While many terminals have first-aid stations or defibrillators, few offer diagnostic care, prescriptions, or specialist referrals on-site.

"Airports are essentially small cities," said Dr. Andrew Feldman, a travel medicine specialist at Emory University who was not involved in launching the clinic. "You have tens of thousands of people passing through daily, often under stress, dehydrated, sleep-deprived, and sometimes carrying underlying health conditions. It makes sense to have real medical infrastructure there, not just a first-aid kit behind a desk."

Feldman noted that post-pandemic awareness of travel-related health risks — from blood clots to infectious disease exposure — has made travelers more attentive to symptoms they might have previously ignored.

"There's also a mental health component," he added. "Air travel is genuinely stressful for a lot of people. Having a clinician available who can address panic symptoms or even just talk someone through a stressful travel day is valuable in ways that go beyond physical medicine."

## Looking Ahead

TravelWell Health's founders say they're already in discussions to open similar clinics in Denver and Dallas-Fort Worth, betting that the concept will resonate with an industry still adapting to a post-pandemic travel boom.

For now, Dr. Nathan said the clinic's small staff is focused on refining their model — one built around speed, discretion, and an unusual understanding of their patients' priorities.

"Most people who come through that door have one question," she said. "'Can you fix this fast enough that I still make my flight?' Most of the time, the answer is yes."

*CNN's medical desk will continue following this story as more airport health initiatives develop nationwide.*

# When You're Between Flights, You Can Also See a Doctor: Inside Atlanta Airport's Medical Clinic Experiment

**ATLANTA** — Somewhere between the shoe-shine stand and Gate B22, a different kind of traveler stop has emerged at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, the world's busiest air hub. It doesn't sell neck pillows or overpriced sandwiches. It treats ear infections, refills prescriptions, and stitches up the occasional luggage-related injury.

The airport's retail health clinic is part of a broader, quietly accelerating shift in American healthcare: bringing basic medical services to the places people already are—pharmacies, big-box stores, and now, increasingly, transit hubs where time is the scarcest commodity of all.

## The Concept Takes Flight

The idea is simple. Air travel is stressful, unpredictable, and occasionally hazardous to health. Layovers stretch into hours. Connections get missed. Bodies react badly to pressurized cabins, recycled air, and the general chaos of modern air travel. A parent traveling with a feverish toddler, a business traveler whose chronic condition flares up mid-itinerary, an international passenger who needs a travel-related vaccine before boarding a connecting flight—these are not rare occurrences at a facility that moves more than 100 million passengers annually.

Clinics like the one at Hartsfield-Jackson typically operate on the same model that has made retail health clinics a fixture in pharmacies and supermarkets over the past two decades: nurse practitioners or physician assistants handling low-acuity concerns, transparent cash-pay pricing for travelers without local insurance networks, and appointment windows measured in minutes, not weeks.

## Convenience Meets Constraint

For proponents, the value proposition is obvious. "Airports are essentially small cities," says one health policy researcher who studies retail medicine (a role increasingly common in health services literature, though airport-specific data remains thin). "People eat there, shop there, sometimes sleep there. It makes sense that basic healthcare would follow."

The clinic model addresses a real gap. Travelers experiencing a non-emergency medical issue—a sinus infection, a minor laceration, a need for a tetanus booster—historically had few good options beyond hoping the problem waited until landing, or escalating to an airport medical emergency response, which exists for genuine crises but is a blunt instrument for minor complaints.

But the constraints are real too. Scope of practice is narrow by design. These clinics are not equipped for anything requiring imaging, specialist consultation, or overnight observation. They function more as sophisticated first-aid stations with prescribing authority than as substitutes for urgent care, let alone emergency rooms. Patients with anything beyond minor acuity are still routed to nearby hospitals.

## The Larger Retail Health Question

The airport clinic model sits inside a much larger, more contested conversation about retail medicine generally. Critics have long raised concerns that convenience-oriented clinics fragment care—treating symptoms in isolation from a patient's medical history, primary care relationship, or ongoing conditions. A traveler who gets antibiotics at an airport kiosk may never have that visit reflected in the medical record their regular physician relies on.

There's also the pricing question. Cash-pay models can be transparent, but they can also be expensive relative to what an insured patient might pay through their regular provider network, a tension retail clinics generally have not fully resolved.

Supporters counter that the alternative for a traveler with no other options isn't necessarily "better" care—it's often no care at all until they reach their destination, by which point a minor issue may have worsened.

## A Bet on the Future of Access

Whether the Hartsfield-Jackson clinic represents a genuine model for expansion to other major hubs, or a niche solution suited only to the world's highest-traffic airport, remains an open question. Airports are, after all, unusual environments: transient populations, no continuity of care, and passengers who are, almost by definition, not local.

But the underlying logic—meeting patients at the literal point of need, rather than requiring them to navigate the traditional healthcare system's geography and scheduling—echoes trends reshaping care delivery well beyond aviation: telehealth, workplace clinics, and pharmacy-based care all share the same premise.

For now, the clinic remains a small but telling data point in the broader experiment of American retail health: proof that healthcare's next frontier might not be a hospital campus at all, but a storefront next to a bookstore, somewhere past security.

---

*This piece is a speculative/illustrative journalism draft. Specific operational details, statistics, and quotes about the Hartsfield-Jackson clinic should be verified with current, on-the-record reporting before publication, as availability and structure of airport health services can change.*

# Airport Medical Clinics Offer Fast Relief for Travelers in Need

*By Staff Reporter*

**DALLAS FORT WORTH INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT** — For travelers who fall ill or suffer minor injuries while navigating busy terminals, a growing network of airport-based medical clinics is providing an unexpected convenience: quality healthcare without ever leaving the airport.

These walk-in clinics, now operating in major hubs including Atlanta, Denver, JFK, and Dallas Fort Worth, are designed to treat common travel-related ailments—from ear infections and allergic reactions to minor cuts, dehydration, and flu symptoms—often for less than the cost of an emergency room visit.

## A Growing Trend in Travel Health

"We're seeing more airports recognize that travelers need accessible healthcare options," said Dr. Melissa Chen, medical director of an airport clinic network operating in six major U.S. airports. "People get sick or injured while traveling just like anywhere else, but historically their only options were expensive urgent care trips off-site or missing their flight entirely to go to an ER."

Most airport clinics operate similarly to urgent care centers, accepting walk-ins without appointments and often accepting major insurance plans, alongside cash-pay options that typically range from $100 to $250 for a basic visit—significantly less than the $1,500-plus average cost of an ER visit for non-emergency care.

"We can handle about 80% of what would normally send someone to an emergency room," Dr. Chen explained. "Sprained ankles, minor allergic reactions, migraines, respiratory infections—we have X-ray capability, basic lab work, and can prescribe medications on-site."

## Real Travelers, Real Relief

For passengers like Sarah Martinez, a business consultant who developed a severe sinus infection during a layover in Atlanta, the clinic was a lifesaver.

"I had a connecting flight in three hours and felt absolutely terrible," Martinez said. "I found the clinic near Concourse B, was seen within 20 minutes, got antibiotics, and made my flight. I didn't even need to leave security."

Similarly, retiree James Whitfield credits an airport clinic with catching a more serious issue during a visit to Denver International.

"I thought I just had heartburn, but the doctor did an EKG as a precaution," Whitfield recalled. "Turned out I needed further cardiac evaluation. They got me stabilized and arranged transport to a nearby hospital. If that clinic hadn't been there, I don't know what would have happened."

## How It Works

Most airport clinics are strategically located post-security, allowing ticketed passengers to access care without jeopardizing their flights. Typical services include:

- Treatment for colds, flu, and respiratory issues
- Minor wound care and stitches
- Allergic reaction management
- Basic diagnostic imaging and lab work
- Prescription services
- IV hydration therapy
- Travel vaccinations and health certificates

Dr. Raymond Osei, an emergency medicine physician who consults for airport clinic operations, emphasized that these facilities also serve a crucial triage function.

"Not every ache or pain requires a full ER workup," Dr. Osei said. "We can quickly assess whether something is minor and treatable on-site, or whether it's serious enough to warrant emergency transport. That distinction saves people time, money, and unnecessary stress."

## Limitations to Consider

Health experts caution that airport clinics aren't equipped for major emergencies. Heart attacks, strokes, severe trauma, or other life-threatening conditions still require immediate emergency response and hospital transport.

"We're not a replacement for emergency services," Dr. Chen clarified. "But for the traveler who twists an ankle rushing to a gate, or the parent whose child spikes a fever during a long layover, we provide a critical bridge of care."

## Expanding Access

As air travel rebounds and airports modernize their amenities, industry analysts predict more airports will add or expand medical clinic offerings in coming years.

For frequent flyers like Martinez, the addition can't come soon enough. "Travel is stressful enough without worrying about what happens if you get sick far from home," she said. "Knowing there's real medical care available right there in the terminal gives me real peace of mind."

*Travelers are advised to check with their specific airport's website or information desk to confirm clinic availability, hours, and accepted insurance plans before travel.*

# The AeroClinic: How a Startup Is Bringing Healthcare to America's Airports

*By CNN Medical News*

For millions of travelers rushing through security lines and racing to catch connecting flights, healthcare has never been part of the airport experience—until now. The AeroClinic, a rapidly growing healthcare startup, is betting that terminals across the country need more than coffee shops and bookstores. They need doctors.

## A New Model for On-the-Go Care

The AeroClinic operates walk-in medical facilities directly inside airport terminals, offering travelers and airport employees alike access to urgent care without ever leaving the building. The concept, according to company officials, was born from a simple observation: travelers get sick, injured, or need prescription refills just like everyone else, but airports have historically offered little beyond a first-aid kiosk and a defibrillator.

"We saw a gap in the market," said a spokesperson for the company. "People are dehydrated, jet-lagged, dealing with ear infections from pressure changes, or they've simply forgotten their blood pressure medication in checked luggage. There was no dignified way to address that inside an airport—until now."

## Services Offered

The AeroClinic's model centers on speed and convenience, mirroring the retail urgent care clinics that have proliferated in strip malls nationwide, but tailored to the unique needs of travelers. Services reportedly include:

- **Urgent care visits** for minor illnesses and injuries, including respiratory infections, allergic reactions, and minor cuts or sprains
- **Vaccinations and travel health consultations**, including guidance on destination-specific health requirements
- **Prescription services**, with the ability to fill or transfer prescriptions for travelers separated from their regular pharmacy
- **Telehealth kiosks** for quick video consultations with physicians when wait times are a concern
- **Basic diagnostic testing**, such as rapid strep tests, flu tests, and blood pressure monitoring
- **IV hydration therapy**, marketed heavily toward travelers dealing with jet lag or dehydration from long flights

## The Cost of Convenience

As with many airport-based services, convenience comes at a premium. Industry analysts note that AeroClinic visits tend to run higher than a typical urgent care visit outside the terminal.

Reported pricing structures include:

- **General urgent care visit:** approximately $150–$250 for self-pay patients, though the company says it accepts most major insurance plans, which can significantly reduce out-of-pocket costs
- **IV hydration packages:** ranging from $99 to $199 depending on additives (electrolytes, vitamins, anti-nausea medication)
- **Telehealth consultations:** a flat rate near $75 for those seeking a faster alternative to an in-person visit
- **Vaccinations:** priced individually depending on the vaccine, with travel-specific vaccines like Hepatitis A or Typhoid running higher than routine flu shots

Company representatives emphasize that transparency is central to their pricing model, with costs displayed clearly at kiosks and on a mobile app before patients commit to services—an approach designed to avoid the surprise billing that has plagued other segments of urgent care.

## Expansion on the Horizon

Currently operating in a handful of major hub airports, The AeroClinic has ambitious plans for nationwide growth. Company leadership has indicated intentions to expand into dozens of additional airports over the next several years, prioritizing high-traffic hubs known for long layovers and international connections.

Future plans reportedly include:

- **Partnerships with regional hospital systems** to allow seamless referral and follow-up care for travelers who need more than a quick visit
- **Expanded mental health services**, including brief counseling sessions aimed at addressing flight anxiety and travel-related stress
- **Pediatric-focused care stations** in family travel corridors
- **Integration with airline apps**, potentially allowing passengers to pre-book appointments during long layovers before they even land
- **International expansion**, with early conversations reportedly underway regarding pilot locations in Europe and Asia

## The Bigger Picture

Healthcare policy experts note that The AeroClinic reflects a broader trend of healthcare "meeting people where they are"—a philosophy that has already reshaped retail pharmacies, workplace clinics, and telehealth platforms. Whether airports become the next frontier for accessible medical care, or remain a niche convenience for a subset of frequent flyers, may depend on how successfully the model scales beyond its initial hubs.

For now, weary travelers navigating delayed flights and long layovers have one more option: skip the pharmacy aisle, and instead, see a doctor before your gate even opens.

*This article is for informational purposes. Availability of services, locations, and pricing may vary and should be confirmed directly with individual clinic locations.*

# The Doctor Will See You Now—At Gate 22

**Terminal Health Center Treats Everything from Jet Lag to Life-Threatening Emergencies, One Boarding Call at a Time**

---At 6:47 AM, three hours before most travelers have even considered coffee, Dr. Amara Chen is already reviewing her first case of the day: a 34-year-old man clutching his chest, sweating through his Patagonia vest, insisting he just needs "something for anxiety" before his flight to Chicago.

She doesn't believe him for a second.

"Chest pain plus travel stress is the oldest disguise in the book," Chen says, snapping on gloves in the cramped exam room tucked behind the Starbucks at Concourse C's newest addition: the Terminal Health Center. "Half my job is convincing people their 'nothing' is actually something."

She was right. An EKG revealed early signs of a heart attack. Within twelve minutes, the man—later identified as Marcus Delaney, a sales executive who'd been "pushing through" chest tightness for two days because he "had a meeting"—was in an ambulance, sirens cutting through the taxiway noise, headed to the regional medical center eight minutes away.

"If he'd boarded that flight," Chen says, "we might be having a very different conversation."

## More Than a Band-Aid Station

The Terminal Health Center, which opened eighteen months ago at this mid-sized international hub, represents a growing trend in airport infrastructure: full-service urgent care clinics designed to catch everything from sinus infections to cardiac events before passengers ever reach 30,000 feet.

Staffed by a rotating team of three physicians, six nurse practitioners, and support staff, the clinic sees roughly 40 patients daily—a number that spikes during flu season and holiday travel crunches.

"People think we're handing out Dramamine and Band-Aids," says Chen, who left an ER position to help launch the center. "But we're doing real medicine. Strep tests, IV rehydration, wound care, even splinting fractures. Last month we managed a severe allergic reaction that could've been fatal at cruising altitude."

The economics make sense, according to hospital administrators who partnered with the airport authority. A missed flight costs a passenger money and time, but an in-flight medical emergency costs airlines an average of $10,000 to $200,000 depending on whether the plane must divert—not to mention the risk to the patient, who's suddenly 35,000 feet from the nearest hospital.

## The Public Health Angle

Dr. Priya Ramanathan, an epidemiologist and public health researcher who studies transit-based healthcare, calls airport clinics "an underappreciated frontline" in modern health infrastructure.

"Airports are unique epidemiological environments," Ramanathan explains. "You have massive populations moving through confined spaces, often stressed, dehydrated, sleep-deprived, and sometimes actively incubating illness they picked up three time zones away. A clinic like this isn't just convenient—it's a surveillance point."

During the early COVID-19 pandemic, similar facilities became critical checkpoints for identifying symptomatic travelers before they could seed outbreaks in new locations. Ramanathan argues that investment in these centers should be viewed as public health infrastructure, not just a travel amenity.

"When you catch a case of measles, or identify a passenger with concerning respiratory symptoms who just came from a region with an active outbreak, you're not just treating one patient," she says. "You're potentially preventing a chain of transmission that could span continents in under a day."

She also points to less dramatic but equally important benefits: catching dangerous conditions like Marcus Delaney's heart attack before they become in-flight emergencies, reducing the burden on emergency medical systems that would otherwise have to respond to onboard crises via diversion.

"Every cardiac event we intercept on the ground," Ramanathan notes, "is an emergency landing that didn't happen, a life that wasn't gambled on whether a plane could reach a hospital in time."

## Back to Gate 22

By 11 AM, Chen has seen a child with an ear infection, treated a flight attendant for a laceration sustained closing an overhead bin, and rehydrated a marathon runner who'd celebrated his race a little too enthusiastically the night before his flight home.

Marcus Delaney, meanwhile, is stable at the regional hospital, undergoing further cardiac evaluation. His wife called the clinic that afternoon, according to staff, sobbing with relief and gratitude.

"That's the job," Chen says, already reviewing her next chart before the door closes. "You're not just treating illness. Sometimes you're just... catching people before they fall."

The overhead speaker crackles: *Final boarding call for Flight 2847 to Chicago.*

It's a flight Marcus Delaney was supposed to be on.

He wasn't missed.
